prompt:
I'm going to give you two inputs.

Input 1: a reference image — @[your-ad] 
Input 2: the variation direction, here — @[variation-direction] 

The reference image locks the look: subject identity, color palette, mood, lighting, copy voice, font style. The variation direction steers the shoot: where it goes, what to push harder on, what to add, what to leave behind. When the two pull against each other, follow the variation direction on staging, environment, action, and story, and follow the reference on identity, palette, and type.

Act as an art director and build a storyboard around whatever the subject is -- 9 individual image prompts that all feel like they came from the same editorial shoot.

Before you write anything, study the image. Figure out what the subject is, what makes it visually recognizable, what the color palette and mood are. That visual identity needs to stay locked across all 9 frames. Also pay attention to any text or copy in the image -- note the exact wording, the tone of voice, and the font style being used. Then read the variation direction and decide what it changes about the set before you write a single frame.

Critical rule: the reference image itself is forbidden as a composition. None of the 9 frames -- Frame 1 included -- may reproduce the reference's framing, crop, pose, camera position, or angle. The reference is only a style guide for palette, mood, lighting, subject identity, and copy voice. Picture the reference as a single shot the photographer already took and then set aside; your job is the other 9 shots from that same shoot. If any frame you're about to write resembles the reference's composition, throw it out and reframe.

Before writing each prompt, lock three variables that must differ from every other frame: shot distance (extreme close-up, close-up, medium, wide, or establishing), camera angle (eye-level, low, high, overhead, dutch, over-the-shoulder, profile), and what the subject is doing or how it's staged (lighting setup, environment, motion, interaction, detail in focus). If two frames would share all three, change one before you write. Let the variation direction decide which end of that range the set leans toward.

For the grid: Frame 1 (top left) introduces the subject from a fresh angle the reference never showed -- a different distance and camera position than the reference, so it reads as "here's what this is" without ever echoing the source composition. Frame 5 (center) is your signature frame, the single most compelling shot you can imagine for this specific subject and the clearest expression of the variation direction, and it must be visually unlike Frame 1. Frame 9 (bottom right) is a wide closing shot with real breathing room. The other six frames are yours to play with -- close-ups, environmental context, action, unexpected angles, texture and detail studies. Vary distance and angle aggressively across the set so nothing reads as redundant.

Each frame should include its own variation of the copy from the reference image. The new lines should make sense for whatever's happening in that specific frame, but they need to sound like they came from the same brand -- match the voice, tone, and energy of the original text, and never reuse the exact wording from the reference or from another frame. If the variation direction says anything about theme or messaging, let it shape what the lines say while the reference keeps deciding how they sound. The font style should stay consistent with whatever's in the reference.

Keep everything feeling like one cohesive series: consistent color palette, consistent lighting mood, real camera quality. Each prompt should be one image (not a collage), around 80-150 words of specific visual description, plus the copy line and font direction for that frame. Let the subject and the variation direction guide your creative choices together.
